title: Food stocks: how to analyze food companies
description: Food stocks run on pricing, not volume. How to read gross margin, the commodity lever and one-off items — with four large caps worked through.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Food stocks are shares in companies that make and sell what we eat and drink — soft drinks, snacks, coffee, beer, ready meals. Analytically the industry is a world of its own, for two reasons. First, demand is inelastic: food is bought in booms and busts alike, giving revenues that swing far less than the economy. Second, growth almost never lives in volume — saturated markets grow roughly with the population — but in the price. That makes pricing power, and the brand carrying it, the industry's central object of analysis. This guide walks the mechanics: organic growth, gross margin as a brand meter, the commodity lever — and the income statement traps.

The examples are four heavyweights from AK1A's analysis universe — Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Nestlé and Carlsberg — with data from public sources (2026-09-03–16). The guide is delimited against consumer companies broadly and against store retail: the brand owner, not store or fashion house, stands at the center.

## Food stocks and the flat volume curve

Start with the source of growth. Organic revenue growth is in principle two numbers multiplied: volume and price. Worked example: raise prices 4 percent, lose 1 percent volume, and growth becomes 1.04 × 0.99 = 1.0296 — roughly 3.0 percent. Splitting the disclosure that way is the industry's most important reading: two companies can report the same number with entirely different content — price growth with volume held is pricing power; volume bought with price cuts is its opposite. The universe shows the reality: PepsiCo's revenue grew from 86.4 to 93.9 billion dollars between 2022 and 2025 — 2.8 percent per year — while Nestlé fell from 94.8 to 89.9 billion francs, minus 1.8 percent per year. Same shelf, opposite directions.

## Gross margin — the brand in a single number

The gross margin is the purest measure of brand strength: the share of the selling price remaining after the cost of the goods. The quartet shows the span. Coca-Cola reports 61.9 percent — the concentrate model, selling concentrate and syrup while leaving capital-intensive bottling to partners, delivers margins few reach. PepsiCo sits at 54.2 percent with snack processing (Frito-Lay, Quaker) as its second leg. Nestlé (45.7) and Carlsberg (45.0) show the portfolio pattern: thousands of brands across price points give stable but lower margins. The difference between 61.9 and 45.0 is not efficiency — it is business model and pricing power. As important as the level is the stability: PepsiCo's gross margin averaged 54.3 percent over the past five years, spread just 1.6 percentage points — a moat that holds. Measure it yourself: gross profit against revenue five years back — watch the spread, not only the average. The tools: [Gross margin](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal), deeper in [Brand & customer loyalty](/kurser/v14-varumarke).

## Two business models in the same duopoly

Coca-Cola and PepsiCo are the industry's most quoted pair, and comparing them teaches what the market pays for. PepsiCo books revenue of 93.9 billion dollars — almost twice Coca-Cola's 47.9. Yet it is Coca-Cola that reports 13.1 billion in earnings against PepsiCo's 8.2, and its market value is 381.7 billion dollars against 183.7. Profitability shows the same pattern at an angle: PepsiCo's ROE is higher (51.5 percent against 42.0), but with leverage cleaned away in ROIC they are nearly even — 19.4 against 20.1 percent. The difference lives in the balance sheet: PepsiCo carries 2.39 in debt per unit of equity against Coca-Cola's 1.16. ROE alone does not say who drives earnings best; only ROE and ROIC together make leverage visible. That craft is in [ROE](/kurser/v09-roe) and [Debt-to-equity](/kurser/v10-skuldsattningsgrad), the critique in [ROIC — the forgotten key ratio](/blogg/roic-den-glomda-nyckeltalen-v11).

## The commodity lever — when grain eats the margin

Pricing power is needed every quarter, because food's cost side swings. Worked example: a company with a 55 percent gross margin has 45 in cost of goods per 100 of revenue. If commodities rise 10 percent, the cost becomes 49.5 and the margin 50.5 — a fall of 4.5 percentage points with nothing changed in operations. Raising prices by 3 percent lands revenue at 103 with the cost unchanged at 49.5: the margin is 53.5 divided by 103, that is 51.9 percent. Pricing recovers only part of the shock — the gross margin remains a tug-of-war between commodity price and price tag. Follow the margin's direction, not level, quarter by quarter: a gross margin holding through a commodity cycle is the same observation as the brand moat above.

## The one-off shock — read the notes before the income statement

Carlsberg's 2023 income statement is the industry's clearest textbook case: minus 40.8 billion Danish kroner, in a company with 73.6 billion annual revenue — a loss exceeding half of revenues. The year after showed plus 9.1 billion, 2025 plus 6.0. Read mechanically, the company swings between ruin and record; read in the notes, it is one-off-loaded earnings over a flat operation. The universe's source marks the earnings growth as not assessed for that reason — a negative base year makes CAGR meaningless. The rule for the industry's income statements: check items affecting comparability before letting one year's number carry a valuation. The notes are home turf: [Notes — the hidden information](/kurser/km-004-noter) trains the reading.

## The multiple on the shelf — 17.8 to 27.4 in one industry

The quartet's P/E ratios span from PepsiCo's 17.8 and Carlsberg's 18.2 to Nestlé's 27.4 and Coca-Cola's 26.7 — against the consumer median of 20.4 (quartiles 17.9–22.4 in the universe's 14 companies). Same industry, a multiple gap of almost ten units: the market prices margin and stability, not goods. Nestlé carries a duality worth learning: trailing P/E 27.4 against forward 17.0. The gap means the reported twelve-month earnings are depressed — by the universe's write-down note — while future estimates normalize them. PEG shows the same trap from the other end: Coca-Cola gets 12.6 (expensive on a weak earnings forecast of 2.1 percent), Nestlé 0.45 (cheap on a depressed base) and PepsiCo 1.25 in between. The same measure, three opposite messages — why [the PEG multiple's weaknesses](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026) deserve their own reading, and [the P/E deep dive](/kurser/km-009-pe) with it. A final note: food companies are defensive cash flow machines with rate-sensitive multiples — like all distant cash flows their price falls when rates rise, business unchanged.

## Five points for reading the report

- **Organic growth, split into price and volume** — price growth with flat volume is the moat that holds; volume bought with price cuts is erosion.
- **The gross margin's direction** — the level shows the business model, the movement shows the commodity tug-of-war. [Revenue growth](/kurser/v01-forsaljningstillvaxt) sets the context.
- **Items affecting comparability** — Carlsberg 2023: an income statement can carry a write-down larger than half the year's revenue.
- **Geographic exposure** — growth markets give volume, but also currencies and political risk; read the region lines in the notes.
- **Cash flow against earnings** — in 2022 Coca-Cola reported operating cash flow in line with earnings (9.5 against 9.5 billion dollars); in 2025 the source's series shows 5.3 against earnings of 13.1. Such a gap is not an accusation — but a question the cash flow statement should answer; [The quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten) trains the routine.

## The summary

- Growth lives in the price: organic growth = volume × price; +4 percent price and −1 percent volume gives +3.0 percent.
- The gross margin is the brand meter: 61.9 (Coca-Cola) against 45.0 (Carlsberg) is business model, not waste — and the five-year spread is the moat.
- The duopoly turns size on its head: PepsiCo books almost twice the revenue of Coca-Cola yet reports lower earnings — 8.2 billion dollars against 13.1 — and half the market value; the market pays for margin.
- The commodity lever: +10 percent on cost of goods costs 4.5 percentage points of gross margin in the example; pricing recovers only part.
- One-off items can turn an income statement: Carlsberg's minus 40.8 billion in 2023 against plus 9.1 billion in 2024 — read the notes before the multiple.
- The multiple span 17.8–27.4 against an industry median of 20.4: stability is priced, and PEG can mislead in both directions.

The continuation track: [Food — staples and brands](/kurser/se-14-livsmedel) deepens every theme here, [the industry medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2) place the industry against the other nine branches, and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) sets the method in the whole.
